text: The deployed lexical-v2 search is useful but weak as a ranked mathematical retriever: Owner Hit@10 is 0.583 and Hit@10 is 0.792, while Source Hit@10 is 0.958. It usually identifies a relevant source but often fails to rank a direct formalization into the first ten files.

The large gap between Source Hit@10 and Owner Hit@10 suggests that file/declaration ranking inside already-relevant sources is a major current bottleneck. Test source-first, declaration-aware, contextualized, dense and hybrid retrieval rather than treating this as established fact.

Frozen multi-query RRF raises Owner Hit@10 to 0.750, and reranking the 30-candidate multi-query pool raises it to 0.958 with Hit@10=1.000 on the current qrels. This demonstrates substantial recoverable ranking headroom, but the reranker remains an experimental cost/latency point rather than a production baseline.

Keep frontend_lexical_v2 as the production baseline while contextualization, dense/hybrid retrieval and reranking are evaluated under the recorded protocol; do not promote the current Cohere prototype solely from its aggregate score.

note: First full-provenance confirmation run after adopting the append-only scientific record.

text: A clean full-provenance rerun of the deployed lexical-v2 baseline reproduces the earlier ranking metrics exactly: Owner Hit@10=0.583, Hit@10=0.792, Source Hit@10=0.958, MRR=0.548, and nDCG@10=0.413. This confirms that the documented weakness is not an artifact of the legacy report format.

The most immediately obvious near-term way to improve search is to retrieve a broader candidate set and then rerank it aggressively. The current measurements make this a concrete hypothesis rather than a generic recommendation: deployed lexical v2 has Owner Hit@10 = 0.583 but Source Hit@10 = 0.958; multi-query RRF raises Owner Hit@10 to 0.750; multi-query RRF plus reranking raises Owner Hit@10 to 0.958 and Hit@10 to 1.000. This suggests that the corpus and coarse lexical retrieval often find the right neighborhood, while the raw file ranking frequently buries the actual owner formalization below import aggregators, adjacent modules, support files, or another file in the correct source.

The immediate architecture to test is therefore: keep the current lexical search as a cheap first stage; retrieve substantially more candidates, probably 50–100 rather than displaying its raw top 10; use modest query expansion/reformulation to improve candidate recall; and rerank those candidates using richer information such as source name, full module/file path, filename, declaration names/signatures where extractable, nearby docstrings/comments, bounded source excerpts, and query terms/synonyms. Display only the reranked top results.

The existing Cohere experiment already demonstrates that this general shape can work, but the exact prototype should not be promoted directly because its cost and latency are not yet acceptable serving targets. A controlled next experiment should determine how much of the gain can be recovered with cheaper deterministic or learned reranking signals. Particularly obvious deterministic signals include penalizing umbrella/import-only files such as Mathlib.lean; rewarding files whose path/name resembles the mathematical concept; rewarding files containing matching declarations rather than merely imports; and distinguishing theorem/definition-bearing files from roadmap, audit, index, and support files.

After that, test an independent semantic first-stage retriever—embeddings, learned sparse retrieval, or another semantic channel—because the lexical candidate-depth audit showed a ceiling: Owner Hit@20, @50, @100, and @150 plateau around 0.625. No reranker can recover an owner file absent from the candidate pool. The measured priority hypothesis is therefore: better candidate generation plus second-stage reranking first, followed immediately by dense/hybrid retrieval; do not wholesale-replace Zoekt, and do not fine-tune a model before these staged retrieval hypotheses have been measured.

note: First clean corpus/file-role quality audit before further retrieval tuning.

text: The corpus currently has a measurable data-quality layer before ranking. The clean corpus-file audit found 209,784 formal-source files plus 10,618 non-formal materialized files (about 725 MB); the Zoekt index contains at least 1,047 README files, 922 lakefile files, 748 lean-toolchain files, and 2,176 PVS .prf files even though the main mathematical search later restricts to formal-source extensions. Within 136,244 Lean files, the conservative diagnostics find 1,514 strict import aggregators. Across the formal corpus there are 3,683 generated-path files, 28,959 test/fixture-path files, 1,335 audit-path files, 56 roadmap/suggested files, and 164 vendored-path files. Exact-content duplication affects 5,198 Lean files (3.82%), including 2,623 files (1.93%) duplicated across source boundaries. In the deployed lexical-v2 top ten, import aggregators occupy 16 of 240 slots across 11 of 24 gold queries, roadmap/suggested files occupy 5 slots, and vendored paths occupy 7. A bounded post-hoc simulation that removes only strict import aggregators raises Owner Hit@10 from 0.583 to 0.625 without reducing Hit@10; also suppressing roadmap/suggested roles raises MRR from 0.548 to 0.575. These role labels are diagnostics, not relevance judgments: most flagged top results remain unjudged, and contains-sorry/admit is explicitly not a safe exclusion signal because a judged direct-owner Serre-duality file contains it.

Before further polishing retrieval algorithms, test whether a cleaner file-level search corpus recovers a meaningful fraction of the current ranking deficit. Keep source membership distinct from file retrieval eligibility: a legitimate formalization source may contain many files that should not compete equally for top mathematical search results. The first controlled intervention should stop feeding material that the main search never intends to search into the Zoekt index itself (for example README/build metadata and PVS .prf traces), then attach explicit file-role metadata for strict import aggregators, generated files, roadmap/suggested files, audits, tests/fixtures, vendored copies, and exact-content duplicate groups. Measure exclusion versus downranking for each role separately against the frozen qrels; do not make a blanket path-based deletion policy. In particular, test suppressing strict import aggregators and roadmap/suggested files first because they already occupy top-ten slots and the post-hoc diagnostic improves Owner Hit@10/MRR without lowering Hit@10. Treat exact duplicates as a separate result-diversity/deduplication experiment. Do not use sorry/admit presence as an exclusion criterion: it is not equivalent to irrelevance or lack of useful formal content. Vendored and test/fixture material likewise require pooled relevance review before any broad filtering decision. Only after this data-hygiene branch is measured should remaining deficits be attributed primarily to candidate generation, embeddings, contextualization, or reranking.

The current bruhat-tits-tree qrels mark chrisflav__bruhat-tits/BruhatTits.lean as relevance 3 even though the file is an import-only root aggregator. Under the documented direct-owner-file semantics, this is inconsistent: the mathematical tree construction/proofs live in imported modules such as BruhatTits/Graph/Tree.lean. Review this qrel before treating aggregator-removal effects on Owner Hit@K as ground truth.

For the primary mathematical retrieval index, unilateral filtering should be restricted to classes with a content-level losslessness argument: (1) non-formal build/configuration artifacts and README/documentation material, provided source-level descriptive text remains available through a separate metadata/docs channel; (2) exact byte-identical duplicate source documents, provided every original source/path occurrence is retained as provenance/aliases so source-specific lookup is not lost; and (3) parser-verified import-only modules containing no declarations or other mathematical commands, provided their import edges and any module-level documentation needed for navigation are retained outside the primary result set. Generated-path, test/fixture, audit, roadmap/suggested, vendored-but-nonidentical, and sorry/admit-bearing files are not safe exclusion classes merely by role. In particular, generated files include many unique declaration-bearing formalizations, and sorry-bearing files can contain exactly the theorem statements that prior-art search is meant to find. This safe-filter boundary should be tested as a data-hygiene experiment before broader ranking changes.

text: The safe file-hygiene experiment reduced the primary Zoekt index from 10,451,699,803 to 9,221,206,550 bytes (about 11.8%) while improving the deployed frontend_lexical_v2 Owner Hit@10 from 0.583 to 0.625. Hit@10 remains 0.792, MRR remains 0.548, and nDCG@10 rises from 0.410 to 0.419. Normalized-content retrieval improves MRR from 0.207 to 0.235. Frozen multi-query RRF retains Owner Hit@10=0.750 and Hit@10=0.833 but its rank-one/MRR quality declines (MRR 0.525 to 0.495), showing that filtering perturbs RRF ordering and is not uniformly monotone across retrieval strategies. The Cohere second-stage reranker retains all success cutoffs exactly: Owner Hit@10=0.958 and Hit@10=1.000, with only a small MRR/nDCG decrease. The production lexical path therefore benefits without loss of top-10 relevant coverage, while multi-query fusion remains a separate tuning problem.

Promote the reversible safe-filter primary index as the production corpus view. The deployed lexical search improves its predeclared Owner Hit@10 metric with no loss in Hit@10, the filtered corpus satisfies the content/source invariants, and every hard exclusion is reversible and individually recorded in filtering/ledger.jsonl. Keep exact duplicates physically indexable for source/path recall but collapse duplicate returned hits through the alias-aware API. Keep the auxiliary README/import-navigation index separate from primary mathematical results. Do not infer that broader path-role filtering is safe from this result, and do not treat the raw multi-query RRF rank changes as solved.

The earlier data-hygiene hypothesis described PVS .prf files as proof traces that could be removed from search. Direct inspection falsified that assumption: corpus .prf files contain PVS proof scripts, tactic invocations, generated obligations, and dependency information that are useful formal prior art. There are 2,176 .prf files in the current corpus (about 478 MB), including 44 above Zoekt default 2 MiB. Filtering decision FD-007 therefore retains .prf as primary formal content and FD-011 forces large .prf files into the physical index. Public query compilation still omits .prf at this point so that the filter-only experiment remains isolated; enabling .prf retrieval must be measured as a separate subsequent change.

A targeted local search for sound_poly_lb_le_ub returns both Bernstein/poly_minmax.pvs and Bernstein/poly_minmax.prf, confirming that the new extension exposes proof-script prior art that was physically present but previously suppressed by query compilation.

Keep .prf in the primary PVS/formal-file query contract. The class contains proof scripts and proof dependencies, its exposure causes no measured regression on the existing benchmark, and excluding it would contradict the project goal of finding prior formal proof work. Treat this as a PVS-specific format decision, not a general rule that every auxiliary prover file belongs in primary search.

text: The first safe-filter implementation classified any basename beginning with README as documentation before checking whether the file itself has a proof-assistant source extension. That is too broad: the live FD-002 set includes formal files such as agda-stdlib/doc/README.agda, Isabelle README.thy theories, ACL2 Readme.lsp books, and Lean README.lean modules. Under the corpus purpose, a formal-source file cannot be removed merely because its basename says README; it may contain definitions, statements, proofs, examples, or other reusable formal content. Narrow FD-002 to non-formal documentation only, regenerate the per-file ledger so these decisions are explicitly reverted, rebuild only affected index shards, and remeasure before continuing publication.

The FD-003 hard filter treated every basename lakefile.lean as build metadata. Audit of the 498 active exclusions found declaration syntax in 125 files: 577 def commands, 13 inductives, 34 abbrevs, 14 structures, 8 instances, one axiom, and one example. These may usually be Lake/build helpers, but filename convention does not prove absence of reusable formal definitions or statements. Under FILTER-004/FILTER-005 this class is too broad for unilateral exclusion; lakefile.lean must remain primary formal-source content unless a stronger content-level classifier is introduced.

FD-004 currently excludes any formal-source extension under an ACL2 .sys directory, but exhaustive inspection of the 9,359 active FD-004 decisions shows that every one is specifically an *@useless-runes.lsp certification report. The generic .sys predicate is therefore broader than the evidence needed for the current cleanup and could silently exclude a future .sys artifact with different semantics. Narrow the hard filter to the exact useless-runes report class; other .sys formal files require their own content-level decision.

The promoted hard-filter classes are limited to zero-byte formal files; non-formal README/source documentation moved to the auxiliary channel; non-formal Lean package metadata (lean-toolchain, lake-manifest.json, lakefile.toml); parser-verified pure-import Lean modules moved to the auxiliary channel; and ACL2 .sys/*@useless-runes.lsp certification reports. Retain all formal README.* modules, all lakefile.lean files, generated/test/audit/roadmap/vendored formal sources absent a stronger invariant, all incomplete/sorry-bearing formalizations, and PVS .prf proof scripts. Exact byte duplicates remain physically searchable at every alias and are collapsed only at the result layer. Future hard-filter expansion requires a new decision ID and the FILTER-004 scientific workflow.

text: Zoekt JSON serving quality is strongly controlled by ShardMaxMatchCount when MaxDocDisplayCount is nonzero. With MaxDocDisplayCount=60 and the final filtered index, the implicit/approximately-300 budget yields Hit@10=0.542 and Owner Hit@10=0.292; explicit budgets 400/500 yield 0.625/0.375, 1000 yields 0.708/0.500, 2000 yields 0.750/0.542, 5000 yields Hit@10=0.792 but Owner Hit@10=0.583 and slightly lower MRR/nDCG, and 10000 is the first tested budget that exactly reproduces the unrestricted local lexical-v2 metrics: Owner Hit@10=0.625, Hit@10=0.792, MRR=0.548, nDCG@10=0.419. The same 10000 configuration reproduces those metrics on the production endpoint. Therefore MaxDocDisplayCount must not be treated as a passive display limit; serving candidate budget is part of retrieval quality and must be versioned/measured independently of UI display count.

text: Deployment audit found that FD-005 did not satisfy its preservation premise. The rule excluded 2,711 parser-verified Lean import-only modules from primary search while claiming that their module names, paths, comments, provenance, and imports remained searchable through an auxiliary navigation index. In production, publish transferred only the primary .zoekt directory; the live Zoekt process was configured only with /home/zack/lean-corpus/index; and no auxiliary index directory was published. Those navigation signals were therefore absent from public search. FD-005 must not be used as a hard exclusion until an auxiliary retrieval path is actually deployed end to end.

Restoring the 2,711 import-only modules to primary search exposes a ranking effect but no justification for hard exclusion. On index fingerprint 76b3312b789850f6c69f98e9fe504625095ba3e16c4a5b1be1a799d807237bf1, raw normalized path/content retrieval has Owner Hit@10=0.583 and nDCG@10=0.408. Stable result-role ordering that keeps ordinary formal-content hits ahead of FD-016 navigation hits recovers Owner Hit@10=0.625 and nDCG@10=0.419 while Hit@10=0.792 and MRR=0.548 are unchanged. The public API reproduces those role-aware metrics. The Cohere reranker on the same restored candidate set remains Owner Hit@10=0.958 and Hit@10=1.000. Direct production checks also return BruhatTits.lean and SphereEversion.lean with FileRole=navigation-import-only, demonstrating retention rather than deletion.

Supersede FD-005 as a production hard-exclusion rule. Parser-verified import-only Lean modules are retained in the primary index under FD-016 until an independently searchable auxiliary channel exists. Production ranking treats FD-016 as the navigation-import-only role and stably demotes those hits after ordinary formal-content hits without removing them from the returned candidate set. This preserves module/path/comment/import discoverability while recovering the measured lexical owner ranking. Any future attempt to move the class out of primary search must first prove, deploy, and measure the auxiliary retrieval path end to end.

text: FD-014's generated-artifact rationale was insufficient for search safety. The reproducible audit filtering/audits/acl2-useless-runes-20260914.json examines all 9,359 nonempty ACL2 *@useless-runes.lsp reports: it records 813,987 top-level event occurrences and, after requiring names to be absent from their corresponding book and then checking all 17,220 ordinary non-.sys ACL2 formal-source files, 589,709 distinct event identifiers remain absent. The production/evaluator query compiler also blanket-excluded .sys, so these generated contracts, induction schemes, signatures, accessors and lemmas were undiscoverable. Aggregate stability on the 24-query benchmark cannot certify this class because those qrels do not exercise the lost ACL2 symbols.

After superseding FD-014 with FD-017, the production index contains 210,723 primary documents and 10,674,992,710 index bytes. The warmed 24-query production run reproduces Owner Hit@10=0.625, Hit@10=0.792, MRR=0.548 and nDCG@10=0.419. More importantly, a production query for APPEND-POLYMORPHIC-SIG returns acl2__acl2/books/acl2s/.sys/acl2s-sigs@useless-runes.lsp, the only matching retained ACL2 file, labeled proof-metadata-useless-runes. The symbol has no match in ordinary retained ACL2 source.

Keep ACL2 useless-runes certification reports primary-searchable under FD-017 and rank them as proof-metadata-useless-runes behind ordinary formal-content results. FD-014 and the older broad FD-004 remain historical vocabulary only; do not restore a blanket .sys query exclusion. Generated provenance is not a losslessness argument when the generated artifact exposes otherwise-unsearchable formal event names. The 24-query aggregate benchmark is a regression guard here, not the evidence that establishes recall safety.

Accept RRB-0002 as a production filtering candidate. The 22 exclusions are exact snapshot-pinned source-local scaffolding or fixture decisions; role names such as test, draft, deprecated, Legacy, FFI, examples, and scripts were not generalized into corpus-wide filters.

note: Post-repository-review production lexical-v2 benchmark on the authoritative remote index after RRB-0122.
Post-repository-review frozen multi-query RRF benchmark on the authoritative remote index after RRB-0122.
Post-review depth-200 control on the canonical remote index; used to measure whether lexical owner recall continues to improve beyond top 20.
First SQ2 lexical-scoring candidate: Zoekt built-in BM25 on the same normalized query semantics, canonical remote index, and depth-200 candidate budget.

text: On the fully reviewed production corpus, frontend_lexical_v2 direct-owner recall plateaus at Owner Hit@10/20/50/100/200 = 0.583/0.583/0.583/0.583/0.583. Increasing the displayed candidate budget to 200 therefore does not recover any additional judged owner file.

Reject Zoekt built-in BM25 as the SQ2 lexical improvement candidate on the current frozen qrels. With identical normalized query semantics and a depth-200 budget it lowers Owner Hit@10 from 0.583 to 0.500 and only reaches 0.583 by depth 50, while Hit@10 falls from 0.750 to 0.708. Continue with genuinely fielded lexical scoring rather than changing the production scorer.

note: SQ2 field-separated Zoekt candidate: deployed path-or-content conjunction, strict content conjunction, and relaxed path channel fused by weighted RRF at depth 200. Candidate generation improves substantially but first-rank quality and latency regress.

text: The first field-separated lexical candidate materially increases direct-owner candidate recall on the frozen qrels: Owner Hit@10/20/50 rises from lexical-v2 0.583/0.583/0.583 to 0.667/0.792/0.833, and source Hit@10 reaches 1.000. The gain comes with worse early ranking (MRR 0.473 versus 0.539), larger payloads, and three retrieval queries, so this is evidence for fielded candidate generation, not yet a production ranker.

Keep the field-separated channels as a high-recall first-stage candidate generator and recover early precision with a cheap second-stage ranker or a less aggressive fusion rule. Do not tune the fusion weights against the current sparse qrels before the post-review pool is judged.

note: SQ2 lexical-v2 reference rerun after Jordan/Hensel pool judgments.
SQ2 field-separated RRF rerun after Jordan/Hensel pool judgments.
SQ2 precision experiment: rerank top-20 field-separated candidates with unweighted SQLite FTS5 BM25 over humanized path and full source content.

text: On the expanded Jordan/Hensel qrels, reranking the top-20 field-separated candidate pool with unweighted SQLite FTS5 BM25 raises Owner Hit@10 from fielded RRF 0.667 to 0.708 while preserving Owner Hit@20 at 0.792. Hit@10 rises 0.875 to 0.917 and nDCG@10 0.417 to 0.421; exact-name Owner Hit@1 rises from 0.167 to 0.667. Aggregate MRR remains below lexical-v2 (0.506 versus 0.553), so this is a useful precision direction but not yet a production replacement.

The remaining early-rank regression is concentrated in descriptive queries where full-file BM25 overweights broad supporting files. Preserve the fielded candidate union and exact-name gains, but next test a structural second stage that scores declaration/signature-local evidence or bounded query-matching excerpts rather than full-file text; keep weights fixed a priori until the pool is judged further.

note: Matched-window FTS5 reranking preserves the fixed field-separated top-20 candidate pool and scores only bounded local source evidence.

text: On expanded qrels, matched-window FTS5 raises Owner Hit@10 to 0.750 from 0.708 for full-file FTS5 and 0.667 for raw fielded RRF, while preserving Owner Hit@20 at 0.792. It does not solve top-rank precision: aggregate MRR is 0.452 versus 0.506 for full-file FTS5 and 0.553 for lexical-v2; exact-name Owner Hit@1 is 0.167 versus 0.667 for full-file FTS5.

The field-separated candidate union is now the stronger recall surface; the next lexical second stage should combine local declaration/signature-like evidence with an explicit exact-path/identifier signal rather than replace broad-file evidence wholesale. Keep scoring choices fixed before the next judgment expansion.

note: SQ2 evidence-fused lexical second stage: equal-weight RRF over path, full-content, and matched-window FTS5 ranks on the fixed field-separated top-20 candidate pool.

text: Equal-weight RRF over path, full-content, and matched-window FTS5 ranks recovers the matched-window Owner Hit@10 gain (0.750) while improving top-rank quality beyond both lexical-v2 and the earlier FTS5 variants on the current expanded qrels: Owner Hit@5=0.708, Owner Hit@1=0.375, MRR=0.594, and nDCG@10=0.497. Owner Hit@20 remains 0.792, so the remaining limitation is candidate recall rather than this second-stage ordering.

Use the evidence-fused FTS5 RRF variant as the leading deterministic SQ2 lexical ranker for the next independent pool-judgment cycle. Do not deploy or tune weights against the current qrels; expand judgments first, then rerun the baseline and all compared candidates on the same gold/index state.

note: Current-gold Zoekt BM25 control rerun for the expanded SQ2 pool.
Current-gold frozen multi-query RRF rerun for the expanded SQ2 pool.
Current-gold lexical-v2 rerun after evidence-fused SQ2 pool judgment.
Evidence-fused FTS5 rerun after its independent SQ2 pool judgment.

text: After independent judgment of the evidence-fused candidate pool, the leading deterministic SQ2 ranker remains materially stronger than lexical-v2: Owner Hit@10/20 is 0.750/0.792 versus 0.583/0.583, Hit@10 is 1.000 versus 0.792, MRR is 0.683 versus 0.553, nDCG@10 is 0.554 versus 0.378, and zero-result rate is 0 versus 0.042. The direct-owner ceiling at 0.792 is still a candidate-generation limitation, not a second-stage ordering limitation.

note: SQ2 depth experiment: evidence-fused second stage over the first 50 fielded candidates.

text: Expanding the evidence-fused second-stage pool from 20 to 50 exposes additional direct-owner recall (Owner Hit@20/50 rises from 0.792 to 0.833 and Owner Hit@10 from 0.750 to 0.792), but degrades early ordering (MRR 0.625 versus 0.683, owner MRR 0.424 versus 0.481, nDCG@10 0.483 versus 0.554, Owner Hit@1 0.250 versus 0.375) and increases latency. Keep the 20-document evidence-fused configuration as the leading ranker; treat the extra 21-50 candidates as recall evidence to judge rather than widening the production-facing rerank pool blindly.

note: Lexical-v2 control rerun after judgment of the deeper evidence-fused SQ2 candidate frontier.
Evidence-fused top-20 SQ2 rerun after judgment of the deeper candidate frontier.
Depth-50 evidence-fused SQ2 rerun after judgment of the deeper candidate frontier.
Current-gold field-separated first-stage rerun after the deeper SQ2 pool was judged.
Lexical-v2 control rerun after independent judgment of the current top-ranked SQ2 frontier.
Evidence-fused top-20 SQ2 rerun after independent judgment of the current top-ranked retrieval frontier.
Depth-50 evidence-fused SQ2 rerun after independent judgment of the current top-ranked retrieval frontier.

text: After independent judgment of the current top-ranked SQ2 frontier, widening the evidence-fused second stage from 20 to 50 candidates exposes one additional direct-owner query in the displayed top 10/20 (Owner Hit@10/20 0.917 versus 0.875), but slightly worsens early ordering and serving cost: Owner Hit@1 falls 0.542 to 0.417, MRR 0.931 to 0.925, nDCG@10 0.678 to 0.627, and median latency rises from 7.52s to 8.05s. Keep the 20-document configuration as the stronger precision/latency operating point; use ranks 21–50 as a recall/judgment frontier rather than widening the display-facing rerank pool.

note: Current-gold depth-200 field-separated first-stage rerun after the top-ranked SQ2 judgment cycle.

text: On the expanded current qrels, the field-separated first stage reaches Owner Hit@20/50/100/200 = 0.875/0.917/0.917/0.917. Its direct-owner recall therefore saturates by rank 50: mapping-cone-quasi-isomorphism and carleson-theorem still have no relevance-3 owner anywhere in the first 200 fielded candidates. The remaining SQ2 recall gap requires a genuinely different candidate-generation signal, not a larger fielded retrieval budget.

note: Current-gold frozen multi-query RRF rerun to measure complementary candidate recall after the fielded plateau was established.

text: The frozen multi-query first stage is complementary rather than uniformly stronger than the field-separated lexical first stage on the current qrels. At depth 200 both reach Owner Hit=0.917, but their two misses are disjoint: multi-query retrieves direct owners for mapping-cone-quasi-isomorphism (rank 13) and carleson-theorem (rank 2), which fielded lexical misses entirely, while fielded lexical retrieves direct owners for dyadic-hilbert-symbol (rank 6) and yoneda-univalent-categories (rank 28), which multi-query misses entirely. A rank-based union therefore has a measured 1.000 direct-owner candidate-recall ceiling on all 24 current queries before any learned semantic index is introduced.

note: SQ2 complementary fielded plus frozen-multiquery union, taking the first 50 candidates from each retriever and reranking the deduplicated union with the existing evidence-fused FTS5 second stage.

text: The bounded fielded-plus-multiquery union closes the measured first-stage recall gap: after evidence reranking it still contains a direct owner for all 24 queries by rank 50 (Owner Hit@50=1.000), and 23/24 by rank 20. The existing content/path-only evidence ranker does not preserve that recall near the top: Owner Hit@10=0.833, MRR=0.798, and median latency=19.9s, versus the narrower fielded-only evidence ranker's Owner Hit@10=0.875 and MRR=0.931. Mapping-cone, Carleson, Jordan, and the Mizar Jordan curve are examples where a relevant or owner document enters the union but is not ranked sufficiently early.

The union's second stage discards the strongest new evidence: which first-stage retriever found a candidate and at what rank. Test a fixed equal-weight reciprocal-rank fusion that adds the fielded and multiquery source ranks as two explicit evidence channels alongside the existing path, full-content, and matched-window channels. This uses only retrieval evidence, not qrels, and should separate candidate-recall gains from content-ranker dilution without tuning weights.

note: SQ2 complementary fielded-plus-multiquery union with first-stage retrieval ranks added as fixed equal-weight evidence channels in the existing FTS5 evidence RRF.

text: Adding fixed first-stage fielded and multiquery source ranks as two evidence channels to the complementary union restores early ordering without giving up the union recall surface: on the current qrels Owner Hit@10/20/50 is 0.875/0.958/1.000, Hit@10 is 1.000, MRR is 0.948, and nDCG@10 is 0.683. Relative to the same union without rank evidence, MRR rises from 0.798 to 0.948 and Owner Hit@10 from 0.833 to 0.875; median latency remains about 20.2 s.

Before any deployment decision, independently judge the new rank-evidence union frontier and rerun lexical-v2, fielded-only evidence fusion, and the rank-evidence union on the same expanded qrels. The main remaining ranking misses are mapping-cone-quasi-isomorphism (owner rank 30), carleson-theorem (11), dyadic-hilbert-symbol (9), and yoneda-univalent-categories (16); latency must be treated separately from retrieval quality.

note: Lexical-v2 control rerun after independent judgment of the rank-evidence union frontier.
Evidence-fused fielded top-20 rerun after independent judgment of the rank-evidence union frontier.
Rank-evidence union rerun after independent judgment of its retrieval frontier; current expanded-qrels quality control before latency work.
Parallel first-stage SQ2 rank-evidence union with two transport retries per API request.

text: Running the fielded and frozen-multiquery stages concurrently preserves the rank-evidence union quality exactly but only reduces median end-to-end latency from 19.68s to 17.62s; p95 is essentially unchanged at 52.38s. The parallel report attributes median 14.57s to first-stage retrieval, 2.61s to candidate-content fetch, and 0.30s to FTS5 reranking, with frozen multiquery dominating the first-stage wall time. Coarse two-stage overlap therefore does not solve the serving-cost problem.

The dominant remaining deterministic latency is serial execution inside the fielded and frozen-multiquery retrievers: three independent field channels and four-to-five independent frozen formulations per query. Evaluate bounded intra-retriever parallelism with recorded transport retries, then compare quality and latency on the same gold/index state before any deployment decision.

Three-worker intra-retriever API concurrency does not improve the current SQ2 rank-evidence union: median end-to-end latency rises from 17.62 s in the coarse-parallel control to 23.03 s, with median first-stage wall time 19.37 s. Owner Hit@10/20/50 remains 0.875/0.958/1.000, while nDCG@10 is 0.708 versus 0.715 in the control; the concurrency level is therefore rejected as a latency optimization.

Test only the lower two-worker intra-retriever bound next. If it also fails to beat the coarse-parallel control, stop increasing request concurrency and move the SQ2 serving frontier to reducing the number/volume of first-stage retrieval calls rather than adding parallelism.

note: Two-worker intra-retriever concurrency bound for the current parallel rank-evidence union.

text: The lower two-worker intra-retriever bound also fails to beat the coarse parallel control. Retrieval quality is unchanged (Owner Hit@10/20 = 0.875/0.958, MRR = 0.948, nDCG@10 = 0.715), while median latency is 20.16 s versus 17.62 s for coarse two-stage parallelism and 23.03 s for the three-worker bound. Additional intra-retriever request concurrency is therefore rejected as the SQ2 latency path.

Move the SQ2 serving frontier from concurrency to eliminating redundant first-stage work. The fielded baseline channel and the original frozen-multiquery formulation compile to the same deployed normalized path/content request, so coalescing that request once per query should reduce first-stage request count without changing either retriever's mathematical semantics or using qrels for tuning. Measure exact ranking identity and latency from a committed implementation before any production decision.

note: SQ2 request-coalescing experiment: share the one identical deployed normalized path/content request used by fielded and frozen-multiquery first stages.

text: Coalescing the one identical fielded-baseline/frozen-multiquery API request per query preserves every recorded top-result ranking exactly on all 24 cases and leaves all ranking metrics unchanged. It reduces physical first-stage requests from 179 to 155 (24 fewer; 13.4%) and total recorded payload from 507,153,995 to 462,726,107 bytes, but median latency is 18.13 s versus 17.62 s in the coarse-parallel control; the lower single-run p95 (47.22 s versus 52.38 s) is insufficient evidence of a latency gain.

Keep request coalescing as a semantics-preserving efficiency improvement, but move the next SQ2 serving experiment to response-volume reduction. The union only consumes the top 50 from each fused first stage while every constituent API request currently asks for 200 results; test a fixed depth-100 bound first and require owner-recall/ranking preservation before considering depth 50. This changes candidate-generation depth and must therefore be measured as retrieval behavior, not assumed safe.

note: SQ2 response-depth experiment: cap every first-stage API response at 100 files while preserving the current coalesced fielded+frozen-multiquery union and top-50-per-retriever candidate union.

text: Reducing each first-stage API response from 200 to 100 files preserves Owner Hit@10/20/50/100 at 0.875/0.958/1.000/1.000, but it does not preserve ranking: 11 of 24 query result lists change, fundamental-group-covering-space moves its first owner from rank 1 to 2, Owner MRR falls from 0.662 to 0.641, and nDCG@10 from 0.715 to 0.708. Mean payload falls from 19.28 MB/query to 16.05 MB/query, but median latency is 19.53 s versus 18.13 s in the depth-200 coalesced control. The fixed depth-100 cap therefore fails the predeclared exact-ranking-preservation condition.

Do not continue to a depth-50 response cap. The first-stage rankers need ordered file identities but not source snippets, while the second stage fetches candidate contents separately. Test a transport-only first-stage mode with ChunkMatches disabled at the existing depth-200 budget; require exact file-ranking identity and measure payload/latency before considering it for the serving path.

note: SQ2 transport-only first-stage experiment: keep the depth-200 coalesced fielded+frozen-multiquery retrieval semantics, but omit Zoekt ChunkMatches from first-stage responses because candidate contents are fetched separately by the second stage.

text: Omitting first-stage ChunkMatches preserves Owner Hit@1/5/10/20/50, Owner MRR, Hit@10, and MRR exactly relative to the depth-200 coalesced control; mean payload falls from 19.28 MB/query to 16.93 MB/query. End-to-end latency is not improved convincingly (p50 18.36 s versus 18.13 s; p95 49.71 s versus 47.22 s). Three of 24 complete ranked file lists differ across the two end-to-end runs despite unchanged owner metrics, so historical-run comparison does not establish exact ordering identity.

Resolve whether the three changed ranked lists are caused by ChunkMatches or ordinary API tie/order variation with a paired same-index request diagnostic. Compare each unique current first-stage query immediately with ChunkMatches enabled and disabled, preserving every other request option, and test ordered file identities/scores directly before accepting or rejecting chunkless first-stage transport.

note: Paired same-index diagnostic comparing ChunkMatches enabled versus disabled for every unique current SQ2 first-stage query.

text: Chunkless first-stage transport is not semantics-preserving on the deployed Zoekt service. In the paired same-index population, 15 of 155 unique first-stage queries changed ordered file identities and scores when ChunkMatches was disabled; each mismatch repeated twice with the same chunked and chunkless rankings, so this is a stable option effect rather than ordinary tie/order drift. Payload fell by 15.3%, but the transport optimization changes retrieval behavior and is rejected.

Retain ChunkMatches for SQ2 first-stage retrieval and evaluate the already-implemented server-batched transport with chunks enabled. Batching coalesces identical fielded/multiquery requests and reduces HTTP round trips without changing the compiled search population; the next measurement must verify ranking quality and end-to-end latency on the same current gold/index state.

note: Bounded server-batched SQ2 first-stage transport with ChunkMatches retained, batch size 3, and server concurrency 2.

text: Bounded server batching preserves the current SQ2 rank-evidence retrieval result exactly: all 24 ranked top-result lists match the unbatched, coarse-parallel, and coalesced controls, with Owner Hit@10/20/50 = 0.875/0.958/1.000, MRR = 0.948, and nDCG@10 = 0.715. It reduces first-stage HTTP transport requests to 62 for the same 155 backend searches (versus 155 physical requests in the coalesced control) and lowers the single-run median end-to-end latency to 15.30 s from 18.13 s, but p95 rises to 65.84 s because several expensive batches have severe cold-cache tails. Keep bounded batching as a semantics-preserving transport improvement; do not treat this one run as proof of tail-latency improvement.

The remaining SQ2 serving problem is now dominated by backend search cost and cold-cache tail latency rather than HTTP request count: batching reduced transport calls without changing rankings, while Hensel, sphere eversion, Pontryagin duality, and formal-group queries still produced 57-100 s first-stage walls. After the cache TTL has naturally expired, measure the same bounded batches at server concurrency 1 before deciding whether batching should be retained; if tail behavior does not improve, stop transport tuning and move to a cheaper complementary lexical candidate generator that reduces the 155 backend searches themselves.

Cold-cache bounded batching at server concurrency 1 is operationally worse: the run completed five cases, then the Hensel complete-DVR batch returned HTTP 504 on all three configured attempts after more than three minutes. The concurrency-1 transport setting therefore fails the SQ2 serving requirement before a complete 24-case quality/latency measurement can be produced.

Stop transport-concurrency tuning for SQ2. Concurrency 2 already preserves ranking but has severe cold-cache tails, while concurrency 1 times out on the Hensel case. Preserve bounded batching as an optional semantics-preserving transport mechanism, and move the active frontier to reducing the 155 backend searches in the complementary lexical candidate generator.

Test a deterministic OR-compressed frozen-expansion retriever: compile every frozen formulation exactly as today and combine the complete compiled branches into one parenthesized Zoekt OR expression. This uses one complementary backend search per case instead of one search per formulation while retaining all frozen expansion vocabulary and each branch's file/case filters; evaluate it without qrel-driven term selection and reject it unless the fielded+compressed union retains the current owner-recall advantage.

OR-compressing the frozen expansion formulations is not operationally viable on the current Zoekt backend: the run completed five cases, then the Hensel complete-DVR OR query timed out on all three configured attempts (92 s batch timeout per attempt). The candidate therefore fails before a complete quality measurement can be produced.

Reject the OR-compressed frozen-expansion candidate. It reduces nominal backend-query count but creates a single pathological disjunction that is slower than the bounded independent searches on the Hensel case. Preserve the frozen formulations as independent evidence when used; move the SQ2 frontier to a complementary lexical generator whose cost does not scale as one expensive Zoekt search per formulation.

Before introducing a new lexical engine, test a fixed one-expansion prefix of the existing frozen multi-query generator: for every query keep the original formulation plus exactly the first frozen expansion, with no per-query selection or qrel-dependent term choice. In the batched fielded union this should cut the first-stage population from 155 backend searches to at most 96 while preserving the same ranking machinery. Accept it only if the union retains the current 1.000 direct-owner candidate recall by rank 50 and does not materially degrade the rank-evidence top-10 metrics; otherwise reject the truncation rather than tuning a per-query expansion count.

A fixed one-expansion prefix of frozen multi-query is not operationally viable on the current Zoekt backend: with the same bounded server-batched transport (batch size 3, concurrency 2, 92 s request timeout, two retries), the run completed five cases and then the Hensel complete-DVR case returned HTTP 504 on all three attempts. This truncation therefore fails before a complete 24-case quality measurement can be produced.

Reject fixed-prefix truncation as the SQ2 complementary lexical generator. Even the original formulation plus one fixed expansion still inherits the pathological Hensel backend-search cost and cannot satisfy the serving requirement. Do not tune per-query expansion counts; move to an independent mature lexical engine whose first-stage cost does not require one expensive Zoekt search per formulation.

Evaluate a corpus-wide SQLite FTS5/BM25-family first-stage index as the next lexical candidate, using deterministic fields and the existing canonical filtered corpus metadata. Build it from a bounded streamed corpus representation rather than rehydrating all source trees at once; compare owner recall at 10/20/50/100/200, exact-name behavior, latency, and storage against lexical-v2 and the current fielded Zoekt union.

note: Corpus-wide contentless SQLite FTS5 BM25-family first-stage candidate at depth 200 on the canonical post-review corpus.
Equal-weight source/path/content field-separated FTS5 RRF control at depth 200 on the same corpus-wide index.

text: Corpus-wide SQLite FTS5 BM25 is a viable independent SQ2 first stage on the canonical 201,221-document corpus: Owner Hit@10/20/50/100/200 is 0.792/0.875/0.917/0.958/0.958, Hit@10 is 0.958, and query latency is 179 ms p50 / 429 ms p95. The contentless index occupies about 1.21 GB. It is substantially cheaper than the frozen multi-query Zoekt path while adding owner candidates beyond lexical-v2, but it does not match the current rank-evidence union at top 10.

Reject equal-weight source/path/content FTS5 field RRF as an SQ2 ranking candidate: on the same index and qrels it lowers Owner Hit@10 from 0.792 for corpus BM25 to 0.458 and nDCG@10 from 0.456 to 0.221. Retain the simpler corpus-wide BM25 run as the independent lexical candidate source.

Replace the expensive frozen multi-query complement in the current SQ2 union with the independent corpus-wide FTS5 BM25 candidate stream. Fuse it with the existing field-separated Zoekt first stage and the established candidate-content evidence ranker using fixed rank evidence, with no qrel-driven weight tuning. This should preserve complementary owner recall while reducing first-stage Zoekt searches from the 155-query multi-query population to the three field channels per benchmark query; measure owner recall at 10/20/50/100/200, exact-name behavior, latency, and new pool members before any production choice.

note: SQ2 hybrid lexical candidate: field-separated Zoekt plus independent corpus-wide FTS5 BM25, 100 files per retriever, candidate-content evidence RRF, and fixed first-stage rank evidence.

text: Replacing frozen multi-query expansion with corpus-wide FTS5 BM25 materially improves the current SQ2 union while eliminating the expansion-search population. With fixed 100-file prefixes from fielded Zoekt and corpus FTS5, candidate-content evidence RRF plus first-stage rank evidence reaches Owner Hit@10/20/50 = 0.958/1.000/1.000, Hit@10 = 1.000, MRR = 0.907, and nDCG@10 = 0.662. The six exact-name cases retain Owner Hit@5/10 = 1.000. This exceeds the prior frozen-multiquery rank-evidence union on Owner Hit@10/20 (0.875/0.958) while using three Zoekt field searches plus one server-local FTS5 query per case instead of the multi-query search population.

The hybrid prototype is still too expensive as a serving shape because it reranks nearly the full 200-file union: median fielded retrieval is about 6.23 s, candidate-content fetch about 5.08 s for a median 179.5 files, corpus FTS5 itself only about 0.13 s, and reranking about 0.57 s. The reported 13.15 s p50 is a component sum and excludes a production network path for corpus FTS5. The dominant reducible cost is therefore candidate volume and Zoekt field retrieval, not the new FTS5 query.

Test the same hybrid with a fixed 50-file prefix from each first-stage retriever. This is the predeclared bounded-pool size already used by the prior union and should roughly halve content fetch/rerank volume. Accept the reduction only if Owner Hit@10 remains 0.958, Owner Hit@20 remains 1.000, and the exact-name slice retains Owner Hit@10 = 1.000; otherwise keep the depth-100 hybrid and investigate a different serving optimization rather than tuning per query.

note: Predeclared SQ2 bounded-pool experiment: fixed 50-file prefixes from both fielded Zoekt and corpus-wide FTS5, with unchanged evidence-RRF and first-stage rank evidence.

text: Halving each hybrid first-stage prefix from 100 to 50 reduces mean end-to-end component latency from 13.15 s to 9.21 s, p95 from 33.56 s to 28.45 s, aggregate content-fetch wall time from 135.8 s to 64.0 s, and fetched candidate-content bytes from 147.7 MB to 87.7 MB. It fails the predeclared retrieval gate: Owner Hit@10 falls from 0.958 to 0.917 and Owner Hit@20 from 1.000 to 0.958, although the six exact-name cases retain Owner Hit@10 = 1.000.

Reject the fixed 50-per-retriever hybrid as the SQ2 operating point because it loses one direct-owner query from both the top 10 and top 20 against the predeclared acceptance criteria. Keep the 100-per-retriever hybrid as the retrieval-quality reference; reduce second-stage work without truncating either retriever before their rank evidence has been combined.

Preserve the established 100-file prefix from each first-stage retriever, fuse only their qrel-independent first-stage ranks, and preselect a fixed 100-document second-stage pool before fetching source content. This keeps ranks 51-100 available to contribute complementary evidence while bounding content fetch and evidence reranking. Accept only if Owner Hit@10 remains 0.958, Owner Hit@20 remains 1.000, the exact-name slice keeps Owner Hit@10 = 1.000, and content-fetch volume materially falls.

note: SQ2 qrel-independent rank-prefilter experiment: preserve 100-file prefixes from both first-stage retrievers, fuse their ranks, and bound source-content fetch/rerank to a fixed 100-document second-stage pool.

text: First-stage rank prefiltering preserves the 100-file prefix from each retriever and cuts fetched candidate-content bytes from 147.7 MB to 95.0 MB, aggregate content-fetch wall time from 135.8 s to 78.1 s, and median component latency from 13.15 s to 10.85 s. Owner Hit@10 remains 0.958 and the exact-name slice remains 1.000, but Owner Hit@20 falls from 1.000 to 0.958: mapping-cone-quasi-isomorphism moves from owner rank 19 in the full hybrid to rank 41 after the 100-document prefilter.

Reject the 100-document first-stage-rank prefilter as the SQ2 operating point. It fails the predeclared Owner Hit@20 = 1.000 condition despite useful fetch savings. Retain the full 100-per-retriever hybrid as the retrieval-quality reference; do not shrink the evidence population before content scoring.

The remaining reducible cost in the accepted hybrid is now content transport rather than corpus FTS5 retrieval. Keep the full candidate/evidence population fixed and test only higher parallelism in exact source-content fetches. This is semantics-preserving by construction if every requested repository/path returns the same indexed bytes; require identical ranked results and current Owner Hit@10/20 plus exact-name metrics, then compare fetch wall time and p95 latency.

note: SQ2 source-content transport experiment: full 100-per-retriever hybrid, unchanged ranking/evidence population, exact candidate-content fetch concurrency raised from 8 to 16 workers.

text: Raising exact candidate-content fetch parallelism from 8 to 16 workers preserves the accepted hybrid ranking exactly through the recorded top 20 for all 24 benchmark queries and leaves Owner Hit@10/20/50 = 0.958/1.000/1.000, Hit@10 = 1.000, MRR = 0.907, and nDCG@10 = 0.662 unchanged. Aggregate content-fetch wall time falls from 135.8 s to 74.8 s; median component latency falls from 13.15 s to 10.56 s and p95 from 33.56 s to 23.44 s, with identical fetched bytes.

Use 16 concurrent exact-file fetch workers as the SQ2 experimental operating point for the current hybrid. The change is transport-only and reproduced the accepted ranking exactly while materially reducing content-fetch wall time. This does not yet imply a production serving default; any deployed content endpoint must still enforce bounded concurrency and verify byte identity.

The remaining expensive first-stage component is the three-channel field-separated Zoekt retrieval. Test a cheaper complementary pair consisting of one deployed lexical-v2 Zoekt ranking plus the independent corpus-wide FTS5 BM25 ranking, keeping the same 100-file prefix from each retriever, full content-evidence reranking, first-stage rank evidence, and 16 exact-content fetch workers. This removes two Zoekt searches per query without qrel-driven selection. Accept it only if Owner Hit@10 remains 0.958, Owner Hit@20 remains 1.000, the exact-name slice keeps Owner Hit@10 = 1.000, and first-stage/overall latency materially improves; otherwise retain field-separated Zoekt as the complement.

note: SQ2 cheaper first-stage ablation: replace three-channel fielded Zoekt with deployed lexical-v2 while retaining corpus-wide FTS5 BM25, 100-file prefixes, full content-evidence reranking, fixed first-stage rank evidence, and 16 exact-content fetch workers.

text: Replacing the three-channel field-separated Zoekt complement with one deployed lexical-v2 ranking is cheaper but loses the accepted hybrid quality. Owner Hit@10/20 falls from 0.958/1.000 to 0.875/0.958, Hit@10 falls from 1.000 to 0.958, and nDCG@10 from 0.662 to 0.611. Owner Hit@50 remains 1.000 and all six exact-name cases remain within the top 10. Median component latency falls only from 10.56 s to 9.95 s while p95 rises from 23.44 s to 24.89 s, so the quality loss is not offset by a robust latency gain.

Reject lexical-v2 plus corpus FTS5 as the SQ2 operating point. It fails the predeclared Owner Hit@10 = 0.958 and Owner Hit@20 = 1.000 gates. Retain the field-separated Zoekt plus corpus FTS5 hybrid as the retrieval-quality reference with 16 exact-content fetch workers.

The field-separated Zoekt complement is necessary relative to lexical-v2 alone, but its three channels may not all be necessary. Evaluate fixed one-channel removals from the established baseline/content/path field set, with all other hybrid settings unchanged and without qrel-driven weight tuning. A two-channel candidate may replace the three-channel complement only if it preserves Owner Hit@10 = 0.958, Owner Hit@20 = 1.000, the exact-name slice Owner Hit@10 = 1.000, and materially reduces Zoekt first-stage cost; otherwise keep all three channels and move beyond Zoekt transport tuning.

note: SQ2 fixed channel ablation: fielded Zoekt baseline+content plus corpus FTS5, retaining established weights and evidence reranking.

text: Removing the path channel from the fielded Zoekt complement fails the predeclared retrieval gates: Owner Hit@10/20 drops from 0.958/1.000 to 0.875/0.958, Hit@10 drops from 1.000 to 0.958, and nDCG@10 drops from 0.662 to 0.609. Median/p95 component latency is 10.86/28.48 s, so this ablation also provides no robust latency improvement over the 10.56/23.44 s three-channel reference.

Reject the baseline+content two-channel complement. The path channel is necessary under the fixed ablation protocol because removing it violates both Owner Hit@10 and Owner Hit@20 gates without a compensating first-stage latency benefit.

note: SQ2 fixed channel ablation: fielded Zoekt baseline+path plus corpus FTS5, retaining established weights and evidence reranking.

text: Removing the content field while retaining baseline+path preserves every predeclared retrieval gate: Owner Hit@10/20 remains 0.958/1.000, Hit@10 remains 1.000, MRR remains 0.907, nDCG@10 is 0.663 versus 0.662 for the three-channel reference, and all six exact-name cases retain Owner Hit@10 = 1.000. The fixed ablation reduces Zoekt API requests from 72 to 48 across the 24-query benchmark; reported payload falls from about 240.0 MB to 191.2 MB and component p50/p95 latency is 10.44/21.79 s versus 10.56/23.44 s for the three-channel reference.

Accept baseline+path as the cheaper field-separated Zoekt complement for the SQ2 experimental operating point. Under the fixed one-channel-removal protocol, the content-only field channel is redundant: removing it preserves Owner Hit@10 = 0.958, Owner Hit@20 = 1.000, exact-name Owner Hit@10 = 1.000, and the accepted early-ranking metrics while eliminating one Zoekt search per query. Keep corpus-wide FTS5 BM25, full evidence reranking, and 16 exact-content fetch workers unchanged; this is an experimental reference, not a production deployment decision.

note: SQ2 fixed channel ablation: fielded Zoekt content+path plus corpus FTS5, retaining established weights and evidence reranking.

text: Removing the baseline channel and retaining the strict content+path channels also passes the fixed ablation gates: Owner Hit@10/20 remains 0.958/1.000, Hit@10 remains 1.000, all six exact-name cases retain Owner Hit@10 = 1.000, and the run uses 48 Zoekt API requests across 24 queries. The two passing two-channel variants are not ranking-identical: 17 of 24 result lists differ, so their small aggregate metric differences are not a sound tie-break on the current sparse qrels.

Complete the fixed one-channel-removal campaign with one structural conclusion: the path channel is necessary, while either baseline+path or content+path preserves the predeclared retrieval gates when fused with corpus FTS5. Do not select between the two passing pairs from small score differences on the same sparse qrels. Keep the already accepted baseline+path pair as the provisional SQ2 reference and advance the frontier to independent pooled judgment of candidates where the passing variants differ; revisit the pair only on expanded qrels.

note: SQ2 baseline+path provisional lexical reference rerun after independent judgment of the two-channel differential depth-10 pool.

text: Independent judgment now covers every candidate in the depth-10 union of the two passing two-channel SQ2 variants: 253 pooled query/file candidates, 201 judged relevant and 52 judged nonrelevant, with zero unjudged. Rerunning the provisional baseline+path reference on the expanded qrels preserves Owner Hit@10/20 = 0.958/1.000 and Hit@10 = 1.000; nDCG@10 rises from 0.663 to 0.684 because newly judged relevant files were already in its ranking.

Rerun the alternate content+path passing variant on the same expanded qrels before any tie-break. Select between the two only if the expanded independent judgments expose a robust retrieval difference; otherwise retain baseline+path as the simpler already-accepted reference and advance to a materially different lexical candidate rather than tuning channel or RRF weights on this benchmark.

note: SQ2 content+path alternate rerun on the fully judged two-channel differential pool.

text: On the fully judged two-channel differential pool, content+path remains tied with baseline+path on Owner Hit@10/20 = 0.958/1.000 and Hit@10 = 1.000. Content+path has Owner Hit@1/5 = 0.500/0.833 and owner MRR 0.633 versus 0.458/0.792 and 0.612; baseline+path has higher nDCG@10 = 0.684 versus 0.679 and higher gold Recall@10 = 0.622 versus 0.609. The expanded judgments therefore do not yield a single dominance relation.

Do not choose content+path from its small early-owner gains or retune fixed field/RRF weights on the same 24-query qrels. Retain baseline+path as the provisional two-channel SQ2 reference because it was selected before the differential judgment expansion and still passes every predeclared retrieval gate. Advance to a materially different lexical candidate/pool expansion; revisit the pair only with new held-out evidence.
